iOS for Android developers · Puzzle 4 · 5 of 5

Counting, not collecting

On Android, a garbage collector finds objects nothing uses anymore and frees them, cycles included. Swift has no garbage collector. Here's what it does instead, and the leak it can't see.

Builds on what you already know from Android from the foundation, not on an earlier puzzle here: you can start with this one.

The problem

On Android, you rarely think about freeing memory: the garbage collector, from time to time, finds every object nothing can reach anymore and frees it, even two objects that point at each other. Swift on iOS has no garbage collector. So who frees your objects, when, and is there anything it misses?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Swift uses ARC, Automatic Reference Counting. Each object keeps a count of the strong references to it: the variables, properties and collections that hold it. Every new one adds one; every one that goes away subtracts one. When the count reaches zero, ARC frees the object right away. No collector, no pauses, no waiting: memory goes back the moment it's no longer used.

That has one blind spot. If two objects hold strong references to each other, say a screen holds its view model and the view model holds the screen back, then even after everything else lets go, each still counts one reference: the other one. Neither count reaches zero, so neither is ever freed. That's a strong reference cycle, and it's a leak. A garbage collector would see that nothing else can reach them; ARC only counts, so it can't.

The fix is to make one side a weak reference: a reference that doesn't add to the count. When the object it points to is freed, a weak reference becomes nil by itself. Usually the "child" points back to its owner weakly:

class ViewModel {
    weak var screen: Screen?   // doesn't keep the screen alive
}

The same trap waits in closures: a closure that captures self holds it strongly, so a closure stored on self makes a cycle, which is why iOS code writes [weak self].

The analogy

A library that lends each book to readers and keeps a tally of who has it. When the tally hits zero, the book goes back on the shelf right away. But two readers who each keep the other's book never return either: the tally never hits zero, and both books are lost to the library.

Check yourself

A screen holds its view model strongly, and the view model holds the screen strongly. The user closes the screen. What happens on iOS?

Right. A cycle keeps both counts above zero.

Not quite. Closing the screen doesn't change the counts; both stay at one.

Not quite. There's no collector to notice: ARC only counts, and each count stays at one.

Why does a weak reference break the cycle?

Not quite. ARC doesn't look for cycles at all; the weak side doesn't count.

Right. Weak references aren't counted.

Not quite. It doesn't free anything; it just doesn't keep the object alive.

What's the difference between ARC and Android's garbage collector?

Not quite. ARC doesn't run in passes: it frees the moment the count reaches zero.

Right. Counting now vs searching later.

Sources

  • The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting ("Swift uses Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) to track and manage your app's memory usage… ARC automatically frees up the memory used by class instances when those instances are no longer needed"; "two class instances hold a strong reference to each other, such that each instance keeps the other alive. This is known as a strong reference cycle. You resolve strong reference cycles by defining some of the relationships between classes as weak or unowned references")

What you now know

ARC counts the strong references to each object and frees it the moment the count drops to zero. Two objects holding strong references to each other never reach zero: a strong reference cycle, which leaks. Make one side a weak reference, which doesn't keep the object alive.
